newsitem.title: UK: Sun Life shines after flotation, mergers.
newsitem.headline: Sun Life shines after flotation, mergers.

text.p: British insurer Sun Life and Provincial Holdings Plc on Tuesday said profits rose three percent in 1996 despite the tight pensions and life products market and that 1997 had got off to a good start.

Sun Life and Provincial Holdings, which was floated on the stock exchange last year but is still majority-owned by France's Axa and which groups Sun Life Corporation, UAP Provincial and New Ireland Holdings, said pro-forma pretax profits hit 181.6 million pounds ($293.5 million) in 1996.
Last November Axa announced it was merging with France's UAP to form the world's second largest insurance company.

"We're not a high-flying technology stock but we said when we floated the company we would produce some good solid results and I think we've proved that," chief executive officer Michael Hart said in a telephone interview.

Investors appeared to agree, sending Sun Life shares up 11-1/2p or over four percent to 291p while the overall market was up only one percent. Analysts at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson repeated their buy recommendation.

Sun Life provides life assurance, pensions and investment products to both individuals and businesses in Britain. Hart said he was encouraged by the group's performance in the hotly-contested life insurance market.
Pretax profits at Sun Life Corporation rose 23.4 percent to 110.3 million stg on a pro-forma basis last year while the value of new business rose 21.7 percent.
"The fact that we were able to maintain or increase the value of new business in a very competitive market place was encouraging. There is a lot of pressure there," he said.

Hart said he was also encouraged that UAP Provincial had managed to hold up against a general downturn in the insurance market. Pretax profits there slipped 1.6 percent while net premiums written were up 3.8 percent.
Profits fell at New Ireland Holdings but Hart attributed the drop to changes in accounting standards and said it did not reflect the company's favourable underlying performance.

Hart said Sun Life would now concentrate on shareholder value and core profitability after a year marked by the mergers, flotation and restructuring. Sun Life said it would pay a final dividend of 6.78p for 1996, representing a pro-forma payout of 10.12p and an increase of 10 percent.
Hart said he was satisfied with the group's structure and said he did not see any gaps that needed plugging, adding that Sun Life had made a good start to the year.
"It's been business as usual to date. There is no reason to believe there is any change in the underlying profitability. We are not displeased with the start to the year," he said.

Hart said he saw no dangers lurking from possible compensation to victims of Britain's pensions misselling scandal. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, many people had been wrongly advised by the industry to take out personal pensions instead of staying in occupational schemes.

"As far as Sun Life is concerned, it has a very small exposure. On opt-outs, there are only 1,000 cases and we have made as much progress as we can...it's not an issue for us. We do not believe there is any need to add to any provisions for that," he said.
